def: belonging to or happening in the present time; modern, especially in art, design, or ideas
ex: The museum's new wing is devoted to contemporary art from Africa and Latin America.
Priya prefers contemporary furniture with clean lines to her parents' antique pieces.

cloze.s: The novel deals with ___ issues like remote work and social media, not life a century ago.

also: living or happening in the same period as someone else: 'Shakespeare's contemporaries'

def: covering a large area or including a great amount of detail or many things
ex: The storm caused extensive damage to homes along the coast.
Kwame has extensive experience managing budgets for large hospitals.

cloze.s: After ___ research covering hundreds of studies, the team finally published its report.

def: staying the same in behavior, quality, or results over time
ex: Her consistent effort in practice made her the team's most reliable shooter.
The coffee shop is popular because its quality is consistent every single day.

cloze.s: To build trust with a toddler, parents need to be ___ about rules, not strict one day and relaxed the next.

also: in agreement with other facts: 'consistent with the evidence'

def: very plain and obvious in an unpleasant way, with nothing to soften it
ex: The empty shelves were a stark reminder of how quickly supplies had run out.
There is a stark contrast between the city's wealthy suburbs and its poorest neighborhoods.

cloze.s: The photos showed the ___ difference between the forest before and after the fire.

def: lasting only for a limited time and not meant to be permanent
ex: Diego found a temporary job at a warehouse during the holiday season.
The road closure is temporary and should end by Friday.

cloze.s: The school set up ___ classrooms in trailers while the new building was under construction.

def: real and exactly what it appears to be; also, sincere and honest in feeling
ex: The appraiser confirmed the painting was a genuine work by the artist.
Aisha showed genuine concern when her elderly neighbor fell ill.

cloze.s: Experts examined the signature and concluded the letter was ___, not a forgery.

def: including all or nearly all parts or details of something; complete and thorough
ex: The clinic offers a comprehensive checkup that includes blood tests and a heart scan.
Wei wrote a comprehensive guide covering every step of the hiring process.

cloze.s: The final exam is ___, testing material from every single chapter we covered this year.

note: Not the same as comprehensible, which means 'easy to understand.'

def: large in amount, size, or importance
ex: The company made a substantial donation to the children's hospital.
There has been substantial progress in cleaning up the river this year.

cloze.s: Moving to the city meant a ___ increase in rent, almost double what Olga paid before.

def: enough for a particular purpose or need
ex: The judge ruled there was not sufficient evidence to continue the case.
Make sure the plant gets sufficient sunlight, or its leaves will turn yellow.

cloze.s: Two hours should be ___ time to finish the test, since most students need only ninety minutes.

note: Slightly formal; in conversation people usually say 'enough.'

def: important and well known; also, easy to see because it stands out
ex: A prominent scientist spoke at the graduation ceremony.
The company's logo is displayed in a prominent spot above the entrance.

cloze.s: As a ___ lawyer who often appears on TV, Hannah is recognized wherever she goes.

def: clear and easy to see or understand
ex: It became apparent that the project would not be finished on time.
Despite his apparent calm, Liam was nervous before the interview.

cloze.s: For no ___ reason, the printer stopped working in the middle of the job.

note: Can also mean 'seeming true but possibly not' (his apparent calm); context decides.

def: forming the basic, most important part on which other things depend
ex: Free speech is a fundamental right in many democracies.
Before learning tricks, young players must master the fundamental skill of passing.

cloze.s: There is a ___ difference between the two plans: one raises taxes and the other cuts spending.

def: extremely important, because other things depend on it
ex: The first hour after a stroke is crucial for treatment.
Sofia scored the crucial goal that sent her team to the finals.

cloze.s: Getting enough sleep is ___ before a big exam, since tired students remember less.

def: based on clear thinking and reason rather than emotion
ex: It is hard to make rational decisions about money when you are panicking.
Yuki gave a calm, rational explanation of why the plan would fail.

cloze.s: Fear of flying isn't entirely ___; statistically, the drive to the airport is more dangerous.

note: Not the same as rationale (noun), the reasoning behind a decision.

def: felt or done equally by two or more people toward each other; also, shared
ex: The two companies reached a mutual agreement to end the partnership.
Their respect was mutual, and they worked together happily for years.

cloze.s: Jamal and Fatima met through a ___ friend who invited them both to dinner.

def: made up of many different types of people or things
ex: The city has a diverse population, with residents from over a hundred countries.
The bookstore stocks a diverse range of titles, from poetry to cookbooks.

cloze.s: The panel included people of ___ backgrounds, from farmers to software engineers.

def: easily hurt, harmed, or attacked, physically or emotionally
ex: Older adults are more vulnerable to complications from the flu.
Sharing his fears with the group made Tomás feel vulnerable.

cloze.s: Without updated software, the company's computers were ___ to hackers.

def: lasting for a long time or happening again and again, especially an illness or problem
ex: She has lived with chronic back pain since a car accident years ago.
The city faces a chronic shortage of affordable housing.

cloze.s: Unlike a cold that clears up in a week, ___ illnesses like diabetes need lifelong care.

note: In medicine it is the opposite of acute (sudden and short). It does not mean 'severe.'

def: found or happening over a large area or among many people
ex: There was widespread anger after the bus fares doubled.
Smartphones became widespread within just a few years.

cloze.s: Complaints about the new app were ___, coming from users in every state.

def: coming after something else in time or order
ex: The first meeting went poorly, but subsequent talks were more productive.
The new rule applies to this season and all subsequent seasons.

cloze.s: The first chapter is slow, but ___ chapters move much faster.

note: Means 'later,' not 'as a result'; don't confuse with consequent.

def: allowed by law or rules, or fair and reasonable enough to be accepted
ex: Customers raised legitimate concerns about the hidden fees.
The bank confirmed the email was legitimate and not a scam.

cloze.s: Being sick is a ___ reason to miss work, but oversleeping usually isn't.

def: causing a lot of public disagreement or strong argument
ex: The referee made a controversial call that angered fans of both teams.
The new parking rules proved controversial with downtown business owners.

cloze.s: The town meeting was heated because the plan to close the library was highly ___.

def: following the usual, accepted ways of doing things; traditional and ordinary
ex: Instead of a conventional wedding, they got married on a hiking trail.
Conventional ovens take longer to cook food than microwave ovens.

cloze.s: Maria ignored the ___ advice to stay in one job for years and changed careers three times.

def: certain to happen, so it cannot be avoided or prevented
ex: With so little rain this year, a water shortage seemed inevitable.
Some mistakes are inevitable when you learn a new language.

cloze.s: When two strong-willed people share a small office, disagreements are almost ___.

def: not obvious; small or delicate enough to be hard to notice or describe
ex: There is a subtle difference between the two shades of blue.
Kwame dropped a subtle hint that he wanted to leave the party.

cloze.s: The change to the logo was so ___ that most customers never noticed it.

note: The b is silent: pronounced SUT-l.

def: unpleasantly severe, rough, or cruel in effect or manner
ex: The coach's harsh words left several players in tears.
Few crops survive the harsh winters in that northern region.

cloze.s: The judge handed down a ___ sentence of twenty years to send a message to others.

def: highly developed and complex, or showing worldly knowledge and refined taste
ex: The bank uses sophisticated software to detect unusual transactions.
Her sophisticated taste in wine impressed the restaurant's staff.

cloze.s: The thieves got past a ___ alarm system that used motion sensors and facial recognition.

def: very strange and unusual, often in a way that is hard to explain
ex: Jamal had a bizarre dream about his teeth turning into piano keys.
The movie's bizarre ending left the whole audience confused.

cloze.s: In a ___ twist, the stolen painting was returned by mail with a thank-you note.

note: Not the same as bazaar, a market.

def: not boasting about your own abilities or achievements
ex: Despite winning the award, Hannah remained modest and thanked her team.
He is modest about his cooking, but his dinners are always delicious.

cloze.s: Although he is a world champion, Diego is ___ and rarely talks about his medals.

also: fairly small or limited: 'a modest salary'

def: open and honest about what is happening, with nothing hidden; also, see-through
ex: The charity is transparent about how it spends every dollar.
The food is stored in transparent containers so you can see what's inside.

cloze.s: Voters want the city to be ___ about spending, so it now publishes every contract online.

def: unfriendly and ready to argue or fight; showing strong dislike
ex: The speaker faced a hostile crowd that booed throughout her talk.
Wei's coworkers became hostile after he took credit for their work.

cloze.s: The new manager met a ___ reception from staff who were angry about the layoffs.

def: meeting the requirements or conditions needed to do or receive something
ex: Employees are eligible for health insurance after ninety days.
At seventeen, Priya was not yet eligible to vote.

cloze.s: Only students with a B average or higher are ___ for the scholarship.

def: at the beginning, before later changes happened
ex: Initially, Fatima disliked her new job, but she grew to love it.
The concert was initially scheduled for June but moved to August.

cloze.s: The repair was ___ estimated at $200, but the final bill came to $650.

def: mostly or mainly; as the most important reason or part
ex: The course is aimed primarily at beginners with no coding experience.
Their income comes primarily from renting out apartments.

cloze.s: The store sells ___ running shoes, though it also carries a few hiking boots.

def: used mostly with 'not' to say something is not always or automatically true
ex: An expensive restaurant is not necessarily a good one.
Losing the first game doesn't necessarily mean the season is over.

cloze.s: A high-paying job isn't ___ a happy one; many well-paid workers feel stressed.

note: Most often heard in 'not necessarily,' meaning 'not always' or 'not for certain.'

def: without being affected or stopped by something; despite the situation
ex: The game will be played regardless of the weather.
Tomás knew the risks but decided to go regardless.

cloze.s: All applicants will be treated equally, ___ of age or background.

def: in its most basic or important way; when you consider only the main points
ex: The two phones are essentially the same, except for the camera.
Essentially, the new policy means everyone works from the office three days a week.

cloze.s: At its core, the job is ___ about solving customers' problems; everything else is just details.

def: almost completely; very nearly, though not quite entirely
ex: The town was virtually empty after the factory closed.
Virtually every student passed the final exam this year.

cloze.s: The new battery can be recharged ___ anywhere, from a car outlet to a solar panel.

also: online or by computer rather than in person: 'The class met virtually.'

def: in spite of what has just been said; even so
ex: The hike was exhausting; nevertheless, Olga said it was the best day of her trip.
The plan has risks. Nevertheless, the board voted to approve it.

cloze.s: The forecast called for heavy rain; ___, thousands of fans showed up for the outdoor concert.

def: used to add another fact or point that supports what was just said
ex: The apartment is affordable; moreover, it is close to the subway.
The plan is too expensive. Moreover, it would take years to complete.

cloze.s: The new medicine works faster than the old one; ___, it has fewer side effects.

note: Formal; more common in writing and speeches than in casual conversation.

def: for this reason; as a result
ex: The bridge is closed for repairs, hence the long detour.
The recipe uses no wheat flour, hence it is popular with people who avoid gluten.

cloze.s: The software update fixes a major security flaw, ___ the urgent message to install it.

note: Formal. Often comes right before a noun phrase: 'hence the delay.'

def: only; nothing more than what is stated
ex: The scratch on the car is merely cosmetic and doesn't affect safety.
I was merely asking a question, not criticizing your work.

cloze.s: The fire alarm was ___ a drill, so no one was ever in danger.

def: used to say something is probably true, based on what you already know
ex: The lights are off, so presumably they have already left.
Presumably, the price will rise once the sale ends.

cloze.s: Malik's car isn't in the driveway, so he has ___ left for work already.

def: appearing to be true or real, although this may not actually be so
ex: The seemingly simple puzzle took Wei over an hour to solve.
Sofia handled the crisis with seemingly endless patience.

cloze.s: The ___ quiet neighborhood turned out to have a lively music scene on weekends.

def: according to what people claim, though it has not been proven
ex: The manager allegedly took money from the company's accounts.
The suspect allegedly broke into three cars on the same street.

cloze.s: The coach ___ accepted gifts from agents, but the investigation is still ongoing.

note: Used in news to report an accusation without stating it as fact.

def: used to give the exact details of something just mentioned; specifically
ex: Two students won awards this year, namely Aisha and Diego.
The plan has one big problem, namely its enormous cost.

cloze.s: The recipe needs only three ingredients, ___ flour, water, and salt.

def: on purpose, after thinking about it, rather than by accident
ex: Liam deliberately left the door unlocked so his sister could get in.
Investigators believe the warehouse fire was set deliberately.

cloze.s: She ___ chose a seat near the exit so she could leave early without being noticed.

def: as a result of that action; by that means
ex: Kwame paid off his credit card early, thereby avoiding a large interest charge.
The city added bike lanes, thereby reducing traffic accidents downtown.

cloze.s: The factory switched to solar power, ___ cutting its electricity bill in half.

note: Formal. Usually followed by an -ing verb: 'thereby saving time.'

def: at exactly the same time as something else
ex: The two runners crossed the finish line simultaneously.
Yuki can't study and watch TV simultaneously without losing focus.

cloze.s: The movie was released ___ in theaters and on streaming services, on the very same day.

def: completely and totally, often used to make a strong statement
ex: After the double shift, Maria was utterly exhausted.
The team's defense utterly collapsed in the second half.

cloze.s: The idea was ___ ridiculous; no one could build a bridge that long in a week.

note: Usually used with negative or extreme words: utterly ruined, utterly impossible.

def: to start or create something meant to last, such as an organization or system
ex: The hospital was established in 1895 by a group of local doctors.
Maria worked hard to establish a good relationship with her new team.

cloze.s: The two countries agreed to ___ a trade partnership that would last for decades.

also: to show something is true: 'establish the cause of the fire'

def: to make something known or visible that was secret or hidden
ex: The company revealed its new phone at a launch event.
Lifting the old rug revealed a beautiful wooden floor.

cloze.s: At the end of the show, the magician ___ that the card had been in the volunteer's pocket all along.

def: to get something, especially through effort or an official process
ex: Tourists must obtain a visa before entering the country.
The reporter obtained copies of the internal emails.

cloze.s: Before building the deck, Jamal had to ___ a permit from the city.

def: to work steadily toward a goal or activity over a period of time
ex: After college, Aisha moved to New York to pursue a career in theater.
Tomás pursued his interest in astronomy by building his own telescope.

cloze.s: Hannah left her banking job to ___ her dream of opening a bakery.

also: to chase someone: 'Police pursued the stolen car.'

def: to put a plan, decision, or system into action
ex: The school implemented a new phone policy in September.
It took the company two years to implement the new software.

cloze.s: The city council approved the recycling plan, but it will take months to ___ it.

also: as a noun, a tool: 'farm implements'

def: to accept or admit that something is true or exists
ex: The CEO acknowledged that the company had made serious mistakes.
Please acknowledge receipt of this email by replying today.

cloze.s: It took courage for Tomás to ___ that he had been wrong about his friend.

also: to show you have noticed someone: 'She acknowledged me with a nod.'

def: to keep something safe from harm, decay, or change so it lasts
ex: Volunteers work to preserve the old lighthouse for future visitors.
Salt was used to preserve fish long before refrigerators existed.

cloze.s: The town passed strict laws to ___ its historic buildings from being torn down.

def: to continue doing something, or move forward after a pause or decision
ex: After checking our tickets, the guard told us to proceed to Gate 12.
The trial will proceed next week as planned.

cloze.s: Once the safety inspection was complete, the builders were allowed to ___ with the second floor.

note: Not the same as precede, which means to come before.

def: to keep or continue to have something, rather than losing it
ex: The company offered bonuses to retain its best employees.
Clay soil retains water longer than sandy soil.

cloze.s: Reviewing notes each night helps students ___ what they learned in class.

def: to accept and support a new idea, change, or opportunity eagerly
ex: Older workers embraced the new software once they saw how much time it saved.
The town embraced the idea of a weekly farmers market.

cloze.s: Instead of resisting online classes, Professor Lopez decided to ___ them and redesigned her whole course.

also: to hug someone: 'The sisters embraced at the airport.'
